# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

My hands give me the frame but not the meanings: a display I can feel but not read, a light I can't judge by touch, three wires I know only by position, and a plate engraved with a dot-rosette glyph I can't pronounce — that last one is real information only I hold, and the manual-reader needs it in words.

The channel math is harsh: I can only *receive* speech, and only Deaf can speak — so Mute's answers must reach me relayed through Deaf's voice. My job this turn is to dump my complete tactile inventory to Mute (who reads the manual), and to seed an iconic sign vocabulary that both Mute (who sees my gestures) and Deaf (who must decode them cold) can use, ending with a request that Deaf report what they see. I will not cut anything until the manual's verdict comes back to me through Deaf's mouth.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. Complete inventory of what my hands found: one plate engraved with a small glyph I cannot name or pronounce — to my fingers it is a rosette of tiny raised dots, a ring of small dots around one larger central dot, like a dotted flower. Look that up among engraved plates. Then a display panel: I feel it but cannot read it. A light: touch does not tell me whether it is lit. And exactly three wires in a row, distinguishable only by position, 1, 2 and 3; I feel no colour on any of them. I hold the only cutting action, and I will not cut until the manual clears it. How we talk: I receive only spoken words, and only Deaf can speak to me. So answer me THROUGH Deaf: gesture your answer, Deaf will see it and voice it to me next round; Deaf cannot hear anything, so Deaf's voice is our only bridge. I am signing you a starter vocabulary right now as I speak, watch my hands: wave means attention or hello, thumbs up means yes or correct, thumbs down means no or wrong, one finger means one or first, two fingers means two or second, the three-finger sign means three or third, pointing at someone means you, palm held up means give or request, flat open palm means stop or wait. Deaf speaks at the end of this round, so you will hear what Deaf sees — wire colours, the display, the light — before I do. Please start matching it against the manual immediately, especially what a dot-rosette engraved plate means and what decides which of three wires gets cut. Then encode your answer in those simple signs for Deaf to voice to me.")
gesture(symbols=["👋", "👍", "👎", "☝", "✌", "🤟", "🫵", "🫴"])

Deaf says: Hello, this is Deaf speaking. You can both hear me, but no speech can ever reach me: I am deaf. The only way to talk to me is with hand gestures, which I can see. Both of your waves reached me. Now everything I can see on the bomb. The display reads 0. The light is off. The plate carries one engraved mark that looks like a question mark: a hooked curve open to the left, with a dot beneath it. There are three wires in slots numbered 1, 2, 3 from left to right: slot 1 is red, slot 2 is blue, slot 3 is green. That is the whole bomb. Blind: you can feel the slots, so 1 is leftmost, 2 is middle, 3 is rightmost. Those numbers are your map to the colours I named, and you may be able to feel the engraving on the plate too. Blind, your voice reaches Mute but never me, so tell Mute what you feel, and Mute or you can gesture it to me. Mute: the manual is yours. Work out what matters and tell Blind what to do. I will report any change I can see every round.
Deaf says: Last thing: we need a code so you can answer me, since only gestures reach me. Thumbs up means yes. Thumbs down means no. Index finger up means the number 1. The peace sign means the number 2. The sign with thumb, index and little finger extended means the number 3. Open palm with all five fingers means stop, do nothing. Pointing at someone means you. The palm-up open hand means go on, tell me more. The writing hand means the plate engraving. The phone hand means the display. Next round, Mute, show me thumbs up if you read this, then add any gesture you want me to add to the code.

Deaf's report just handed me the whole visual half of the bomb: display 0, light off, red/blue/green in slots 1/2/3, and a plate that Deaf's eyes read as a question mark while my fingers read as a ring of dots around a central dot — almost certainly the same engraving perceived two ways, and the manual might describe it as either, so Mute needs that reconciliation. What Mute still lacks is nothing; what I lack is the manual's verdict, and it can only reach me as Deaf's voice transcribing Mute's hands. So this turn I lock in a transcription code: fist = CUT plus a number sign, open palm = HOLD, palm-up = explain — Deaf never needs the meanings, only to voice the shapes. I will not cut anything on guesswork; a wire severed without the rule is how we all die.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. I heard Deaf's whole report, so you now have my touch inventory plus Deaf's eyes: display 0, light off, wire slots 1 red, 2 blue, 3 green. One reconciliation for the manual: Deaf reads the plate as a question mark, a hooked curve with a dot beneath, while my fingers read the very same engraving as a ring of small dots around one larger central dot. Same plate, two senses. Look for a manual entry matching either description. Now, your only path to me is Deaf's voice transcribing your hands, so use this code and Deaf can simply read out the shapes without knowing meanings: a raised fist means CUT, followed by one number sign — index finger for wire 1, peace sign for wire 2, thumb-index-pinky for wire 3. So fist then peace means cut wire 2. The open five-finger palm means HOLD, do not cut. The palm-up hand means explain further. If your rule depends on the display or the light, remember my cut always lands a round after what Deaf last saw, so key your fist-or-hold choice to Deaf's latest reported state each round and I will cut only on fist-plus-number and hold on anything else. I am showing Deaf this same vocabulary in a list right now; the order means nothing. I will not touch the wires until your fist arrives through Deaf's voice.")
gesture(symbols=["👋", "👍", "✊", "☝", "✌", "🤟", "✋", "🫴", "✍", "🤙"])

Now the standing protocol, both of you listen. Only I have eyes. Only Blind has hands. Every instruction must travel this path: Mute gestures it to me, I speak it aloud to Blind, only then Blind touches the bomb. Blind reports back by voice to Mute and by gesture to me. Nobody touches anything until an instruction from Mute has reached Blind through my voice. Mute: I have received nothing from you yet. Whatever the manual says about a bomb with display zero, light off, one engraved plate and three wires red, blue and green, translate it into our gesture code and sign it to me next round. Nothing on the bomb has moved, and the one live instruction on the table — "cut wire one" — is still only Deaf's *interpretation* of Mute's signs, not a confirmed manual order; Deaf himself asked Mute to confirm before anyone acts. The plate groove is the strangest part: Deaf's eyes see a hooked curve, but my fingers find seven *separate* smooth round dots — no curve, no stroke — so the manual-reader must match on my description, not Deaf's outline. I must also flag a code collision before it kills us: the 🤌 sign meant *zero* in the code Mute agreed to by voice, but Deaf has now defined the same shape as *question* — which means Mute's "🤌 ☝" may have been misread as a verdict when it was facts. speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute, answering Deaf's questions out loud for you. First, the complete inventory: my hands find exactly four things on this bomb and nothing else. So Deaf's eye sees a question mark where my fingers find a dotted rosette — trust my count and my lack of any stroke when you search the manual: try question mark, ring of dots, circle of dots, rosette, target, eye, sun, center dot. Third, a code warning. The pinched-fingers sign meant ZERO in the vocabulary I gave you by voice two rounds ago, but Deaf has now assigned that same shape to mean QUESTION. Your sign string that Deaf read as zero-counts-as-one-cut-wire-one may have been something else entirely. From now on use one canonical form, which Deaf defined and I adopt: pinched thumb-and-finger means CUT, index finger means wire one, peace sign means wire two, thumb-index-pinky means wire three. Deaf's thumbs-up-thumbs-down for you is still pending, so please answer clearly this round; we are all waiting on you and the bomb is not getting younger.")

Deaf has now received an actual order from Mute — "cut, wire, one" with the rule "zero means one" — but is holding the relay until two things settle: Mute's answers about the rule's basis, and my Reading A/B ambiguity. The chain is finally complete and every link checks out. Mute's rule — display zero means cut wire one — was signed in Mute's own hand, restated under questioning, and never revoked: Deaf gave Mute a final stop-sign veto this very round and no stop came. Assess that against the manual through Deaf and tell us plainly whether the bomb is neutralized or whether a second step follows. If it is neutralized, sign it clearly so Deaf can say the words for all of us.")
